intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 (NSLH1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene (602775) on chromosome 10q25.2.

paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy with a facial appearance suggestive of, but not completely typical of, Noonan syndrome. Affected individuals have reduced growth that is often associated with growth hormone (GH) deficiency, cognitive deficits, a distinctive hyperactive behavior, and ectodermal anomalies. These include easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair (loose anagen hair) and darkly pigmented skin. Cardiac anomalies and a hypernasal voice may also occur (Mazzanti et al., 2003; Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with loose anagen hair and Noonan syndrome. She had short, blond, easily pluckable hair that had never been cut. The trichogram showed an absolute prevalence of abnormally shaped anagen bulbs lacking inner and outer root sheaths. Scalp biopsy showed cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reviewed 19 patients diagnosed with loose anagen hair (14 children and 5 adults). Associated conditions included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy. In all cases the trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80 to 100%) devoid of sheaths. The authors concluded that loose anagen hair may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less commonly, may be familial.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) characterized 25 unrelated subjects with a SHOC2 mutation, all of them sporadic cases. The subjects had reduced growth, frequently with proven GH deficiency, and cognitive deficits. They showed a distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most of them. Their hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing, and loose anagen hair was confirmed microscopically in 12. Some subjects had darkly pigmented skin, eczema, or ichthyosis. The voice was hypernasal. Other features in some subjects were macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, short webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Cardiac anomalies were present in some. Mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. Referring pediatricians felt that several subjects had features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a de novo SHOC2 S2G mutation. He presented with fetal distress that required premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he was noted to have dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. An echocardiogram showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiomyopathy progressed rapidly, and he was discharged for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac findings and other features were not typical of patients previously reported with this mutation, and they concluded that the case expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 male patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay. All 4 with available data had a structural cardiac anomaly. Brain imaging showed relative megalencephaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a small posterior fossa with a vertical tentorium. Four of the 5 patients had initially been suspected of having Costello syndrome. The light-colored, slow-growing scalp hair with dolichocilia resembled the hair seen in Costello syndrome caused by the HRAS gly13-to-cys mutation. Including their own and previously reported patients, Chiari 1 malformation was present in 3 of 8 SHOC2 mutation-positive patients with MRI data. The authors attributed it to relative megalencephaly combined with a small posterior fossa and noted that it can develop after birth.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) described each of their 5 patients. Patient 1 had a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and was born with a cystic hygroma and macrosomia. His course included pyloric stenosis and severe failure to thrive requiring a gastrostomy tube. He also had mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, small optic nerves, and delayed motor development. Examination showed macrocephaly (OFC +3 SD), a large anterior fontanel, sparse thin hair, ptosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and hemangiomata. Brain imaging showed enlarged subarachnoid spaces, a vertical tentorium, mild cerebellar tonsillar ectopia, and a thin corpus callosum. Bone marrow biopsies showed markedly hypercellular marrow with a marked generalized increase in reticulin staining, consistent with myelofibrosis, and blasts were present in the peripheral blood. He died at age 2.5 years after splenectomy in preparation for a bone marrow transplant. Patient 2 was born to a 21-year-old mother and a 40-year-old father after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios, and he had increased birth weight. Macrocephaly, unilateral ptosis, posteriorly angulated ears, increased palmar wrinkling, loose skin, bilateral inguinal hernias, and hypotonia were noted, and Costello syndrome was considered. He had severe feeding difficulties and a subdural effusion requiring drainage. At 9 5/12 years he was nonverbal with intellectual disability, and his height was between the 3rd and 5th centiles. His skin findings included acanthosis nigricans and eczema. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, hypogenesis of the corpus callosum, decreased white matter volume, a vertical tentorium, and cerebellar tonsillar ectopia.

paragraphs.text: Patient 3 of Gripp et al. (2013) had polyhydramnios and macrosomia. Postnatal problems were tracheostenosis, chronic lung disease, and a neonatal seizure. He had right bundle branch block and mild to moderate biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at 6 months of age, as well as aortic insufficiency and mild pulmonic stenosis. Failure to thrive required a gastrostomy. At age 9 years his height was 125 cm (10th centile), his weight 29.4 kg (50th centile), and his OFC 60 cm (+5 SD). At that age he was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome, and he showed aggressive behavior. He also had coarse facial features, osteoporosis, and strabismus. Patient 4 was of Mexican ancestry. He was born at 37 weeks' gestation to a 32-year-old mother and a 41-year-old father, with a weight of 2.9 kg. paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that wildtype SHOC2 was distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells and was restricted to the nucleus after EGF stimulation. Growth factor-stimulated nuclear translocation of endogenous SHOC2 was confirmed in primary skin fibroblasts. The S2G substitution created an N-myristoylation site: SHOC2 S2G incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, whereas the wildtype protein and an S2A mutant did not. The S2G mutant was constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane and failed to translocate to the nucleus upon EGF stimulation. Its membrane localization was reduced by the N-myristoyltransferase inhibitor 2-hydroxymyristic acid. SHOC2 S2G did not heterodimerize with wildtype SHOC2, which excluded a dominant-negative effect. Its expression enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells but not in Cos-1 or 293T cells, indicating cell type-specific MAPK activation.

(2009) identified a heterozygous c.4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 25 unrelated sporadic subjects with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. Four were from a cohort of 96 mutation-negative Noonan syndrome patients and 21 from a further 410 mutation-negative subjects. The mutation had occurred de novo in 3 of the 4 subjects in the first cohort and in all 12 families of the second cohort for which parental DNA was available. The mutant protein incorporated myristic acid, was constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane, and failed to translocate to the nucleus upon EGF stimulation. paragraphs.text: In a patient with a RASopathy and prenatal-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Motta et al. (2019) identified a c.807_808delinsTT mutation in the SHOC2 gene, predicting gln269_his270delinsHisTyr. The mutant protein showed enhanced binding to MRAS and PPP1CB and increased MAPK signaling. Unlike the S2G mutant, it was not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
